name: Cauliflower
summary: Cauliflower is a pale cruciferous vegetable eaten raw, boiled, roasted or grated into rice-like pieces. This page lists what people say cauliflower does and what writers in ancient Rome believed about cabbage sprouts; each claim can be checked against the research when you choose.
inIt: Cauliflower is a Brassica vegetable like broccoli and cabbage. A 2018 review says the family holds more than 200 types of glucosinolate, which the enzyme myrosinase breaks into isothiocyanates.
A 2010 review says Brassica vegetables also hold phenolic compounds, and that processing changes their phenolic content.

The UK food table (CoFID) measures raw cauliflower at 30 kcal, 2.9 g of sugars, 1.8 g of fibre, 252 mg of potassium, 31 µg of vitamin K1, 55 µg of folate and 56 mg of vitamin C per 100 g. It does not measure glucosinolates or phenolic compounds.

lore.who: Ancient Rome (Pliny the Elder, about 77 AD)
lore.belief: Pliny wrote that the sprout (cyma) of the cabbage is pleasant to the taste but is not used in medicine, because it is hard to digest and not good for the kidneys.
lore.note: The Latin word cyma means the young sprout of a cabbage, and the translators render it 'cabbage-sprout'. Whether Pliny meant what we now call broccoli or cauliflower is uncertain, so this is a belief about cabbage sprouts in general.

sources.title: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 20.35 (cabbage-sprouts), Bostock and Riley translation, 1855
sources.author: Pliny the Elder

lore.belief: Celsus listed cabbage, and even more its sprouts, among foods that give bad juice, meaning foods that nourish poorly.
lore.note: The Latin word cyma means the young sprout of a cabbage, and the translators render it 'cabbage-sprout'. Whether Pliny meant what we now call broccoli or cauliflower is uncertain, so this is a belief about cabbage sprouts in general.

sources.title: Celsus, De Medicina 2.21.1 (foods of good and bad juice), Loeb translation (Spencer)
sources.author: Celsus

processing: Boiling cuts some vitamins: the UK food table has 56 mg of vitamin C and 55 µg of folate per 100 g raw, against 30 mg and 48 µg boiled in unsalted water.
A 2010 review says processing changes the phenolic content of Brassica vegetables.

unknowns: Whether cauliflower holds enough goitrin to matter for the thyroid: a 2016 review lists collards, Brussels sprouts and some Russian kale as high enough, and broccoli and Brassica oleracea kale as minimal, but does not list cauliflower.
Whether eating cauliflower changes health outcomes: this page does not review the studies, and the reviews cited here cover cruciferous vegetables as a group.
How much of the plant compounds survive cooking or ricing: the food table does not measure them.
